lessons: Keep the opening hook under 10 words and make it a surprising, vivid statement – videos like “This shark is older than the United States” and “A blue‑fin tuna looks like deep‑red beef” held >1.2 × viewers at 10 % and beat similar videos at start and end.
Avoid dense, multi‑clause explanations as the first line – the biggest early drops (0.13‑0.34 loss) occur when the hook is a long factual sentence such as the garlic or windshield explanations.

Use sensory or paradoxical imagery (e.g., “Fresh pineapple is literally eating you back”, “Gulping ice water after a hot pepper feels like relief”) – these videos kept >1.0 × at 10 % and had the smallest early loss fractions.
If you employ a countdown or pause, place it after the hook and keep it brief – videos with a later drop around 0.6 (the shark) showed viewers leaving when the pacing slowed after the hook.

Repeat key ideas only after the hook has secured attention – videos that repeated the same line in the second biggest drop (e.g., guardrail “instead of impaling your vehicle…”) lost ~0.12‑0.13 of the audience.
End with a teaser or unanswered question to sustain retention to the end – the highest kept_at_end ratios (e.g., James Webb, shark) all finished with a curiosity‑driving line.
worst_moment_types: Long, dense explanatory sentence as the first spoken line
Repeated phrasing of the same idea within the first 30 %
Late‑mid‑video pause or countdown that slows pacing
Overly technical detail without visual hook
best_hook_types: Short, surprising fact or paradox (e.g., “older than the United States”)
Vivid sensory description that creates a mental picture
Provocative question that promises a counter‑intuitive answer
Bold comparison that contrasts two familiar things (e.g., tuna vs. beef)
